source.title: Comparing Latent Concept Formation in State Space Models and Transformers via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Rithin Nagaraj; Rupa Laalasa Oruganti; Prerna Subhashchandra Kunder; Ashwini M. Joshi

page_placements.theme: Correspondence of SAE features across models, finetunes, domains and pruning

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures feature correspondence between two different architectures, but does not test SAE dictionary-size splitting or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper compares Mamba and Pythia SAE features using cross-architecture Jaccard similarity and qualitatively examines selected features. It does not sweep SAE dictionary size or test whether finer features partition a coarser feature's inputs. Dictionary sizes and expansion factors are setup details, not results on splitting. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study compares SAE features across Mamba-130m and Pythia-70m using maximum binary co-activation Jaccard similarity. It uses one SAE per model and no dictionary-size sweep. It never maps coarse features to finer ones, and tests no hierarchy, absorption, cross-size decomposition or training objective. Its only contact with the claim is citing Towards Monosemanticity as general SAE background. The authors argue that dictionary size does not drive Mamba's polysemanticity, but they give that argument qualitatively and do not test it. 'Discusses' overstates the link, since splitting is never discussed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report near-total feature alignment, which they take as preliminary support for universality. They present the Mamba polysemanticity case as hypothesis-generating and confounded by the asymmetric dictionary sizes.
record.recipe_differences: Cross-architecture feature-correspondence analysis rather than a same-model SAE dictionary-size comparison. It uses a pre-trained Pythia SAE and a custom Mamba SAE with different expansion factors and binary co-activation Jaccard similarity.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that asymmetric dictionary sizes may affect apparent alignment and Mamba polysemanticity; its Jaccard category thresholds are empirically derived. It does not report a controlled sensitivity test.

fits_no_version.finding: 99.98% (12,285) of Mamba features had a maximum Jaccard match J > 0.35 with some Pythia SAE feature. The range was 0.2343 to 0.4116, with no null distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-architecture universality: SAE features of Mamba and of a Transformer trained on similar data have high-overlap counterparts.

fits_no_version.finding: A few low-Jaccard Mamba features fire on document-structure markers, such as External Links headers and URL separators.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SSM-specific structural landmark features with weak Transformer counterparts.

fits_no_version.finding: In one qualitative feature pair, a Mamba feature spans varied syntactic anomalies, while its Pythia twin is described as specific to table timestamps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The recurrent bottleneck drives polysemanticity at syntactic margins. This is confounded by the smaller Mamba dictionary.

record.problems: The study uses asymmetric SAE dictionary sizes and acknowledges that the smaller Mamba dictionary could itself contribute to polysemanticity. Its alignment thresholds are empirically chosen without a reported null distribution. The polysemanticity interpretation rests on one qualitative feature-pair case study, and the authors state that symmetric SAE training is needed for stronger evidence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on the listed claim versions were reported. Setup details such as expansion factors and the cited MPPC findings were not recorded as result rows.

untested.parts: No growing-dictionary comparison, no coarse-to-fine feature mapping, and no input-coverage or direction-similarity test.
No splitting pattern is examined in any model or SAE release. The public Pythia SAE is used only as a feature dictionary.
No nested feature families, concept hierarchy or geometric closeness among features is examined.
No parent/child latents, absorption measurement, or variation of SAE size or sparsity.
No comparison of larger and smaller SAEs on the same activations. The Pythia (32,768) and Mamba (12,288) dictionaries are on different models, so decomposition or novel latents cannot be assessed.
No comparison of training objectives. The Mamba SAE is a single L1-penalty SAE.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version. The text has internal inconsistencies. It says '0.03% of diverging features' in IV.B but 0.02% elsewhere. Table I does not show the timestamp contexts claimed for Mamba Feature 4454. The Jaccard thresholds are fixed after seeing the data, and there is no null baseline. The asymmetric dictionaries (expansion factor 16 vs 64) may inflate alignment, so the universality result is weak evidence even for its own claim.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size comparison, coarse-to-fine feature mapping, input partition test, or direction comparison.
The study compares two architectures and uses one SAE dictionary per model, but does not test the splitting pattern across model scale or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families, concept hierarchy, or geometrical closeness of split features is tested.
No parent-child absorption or test of whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes it.
No comparison of larger and smaller SAEs on the same model and activations, nor test of decomposition into smaller latents or novel latents.
No objective comparison or test of whether the SAE sparsity objective produces splitting.

relation.reason: The study cites Bricken et al. 2023 [5] only for SAE methods, but Sections III.B and V.D discuss how dictionary size affects feature granularity. They say the smaller Mamba dictionary may cause polysemanticity and the larger Pythia dictionary may inflate alignment. This is the idea behind V1, though the paper never names splitting. The study has no test, and this does not affect the verdicts.

tranche.reason: The study compares features across Mamba-130m and Pythia-70m-deduped with one SAE per model. It has no dictionary-size sweep and no test of splitting, hierarchy, absorption, cross-size decomposition or training objectives.

source_check.notes: The SAE sizes differ (Mamba x16 = 12,288 features; Pythia x64 = 32,768), which the authors flag as a confound. There is no null Jaccard distribution, so 'Aligned' (J > 0.35) is a descriptive cut. The text is inconsistent on the diverging fraction: 0.02% in some places, 0.03% in IV.B, while 3 features lie outside Aligned. The study has no verdicts and no version links.

statements.problem: None. 99.98% (12,285) with J > 0.35 and the range 0.2343 to 0.4116 are in Section IV.A. The paper says it has no null distribution and leaves one to future work (Section III.E).
